rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: 5 of 6 body headers read as claims ("The move widens to everything you do", "The agent stops where your judgement begins", "You make agentic happen", "There is no last turn", and the noun-phrase-as-claim "The handoff prompt that builds your kit"). Chunk 5's "Ralph" is a bare proper-noun label, not a claim sentence — closest-to-violating header. Checked against corpus precedent: `grep -rn "^## " curriculum/lectures/*.md` shows other short topic-label lecture headers already in house convention ("Bridge", "Eval", "Compounding", "Optional"), so a single-word named-concept header alongside claim headers is established practice, not a drift from rule 15's split (whose measured scope and worked examples are the exercise-imperative-vs-lecture-claim split, not a mandate that every lecture header individually be a full claim sentence). No reader-confusion harm present; forcing "Ralph" into a claim-shaped header would flatten a deliberate closer beat that echoes the bash block below it. Accepted as house convention, not filed as REVISE.
